analysis.title: Four key conclusions from the US midterm elections
key_insights: Democrats won 54 Senate seats and 238 House seats as of 9:30am SGT on 5 November, with a handful of races still uncalled. They lack the 2/3 majority needed to override a Presidential veto, so Trump's authority over tariffs and military action is unlikely to change.

US fiscal policy is likely to swing from a slight boost to growth in FY26 to a modest drag over the next two years. Democrats and Republicans are unlikely to agree on a bipartisan budget, and a Democrat budget with tax hikes or more healthcare funding via reconciliation would likely be vetoed.
Federal spending through FY28 will likely be held at FY26 levels through continuing resolutions.

Political impediments to AI infrastructure spending are likely to rise. Democrats who favour moratoria or other constraints on data center development won essentially all of the races flagged for data center regulation implications, including Ohio, Michigan, Texas, Georgia and Arizona.

Eastspring expects some 2027 AI capex to be delayed but not necessarily cancelled. The debate centres on making data centers pay for their local utility cost impact, pay higher local taxes and give local governments final approval authority. Few politicians argue for outright bans.

Inflation and cost of living are flashpoints across the political spectrum. Political pressure to end the Iran war to lower energy prices is likely to rise, but authority over military action and any truce still rests with Trump.

Eastspring sees a high chance of renewed US attacks on Iran in the near term. Republican support for such action is likely to be short-lived and internal pressure on Trump to end the war is likely to escalate.

The Fed will likely need to be sensitive to the public message that inflation is too high. That may shift its bias toward a more aggressive response to hot inflation prints or signs of rising wage growth than the 60bps of hikes the market currently prices.

The result is a clear public rebuke of Trump. His hand-picked candidates Darline Graham, Michael Whatley and Ken Paxton lost, as did Jon Husted. Eastspring expects Republican legislators to gradually shift support away from Trump's more extreme policy preferences ahead of the 2028 elections.

macro_indicators.reading: Slight boost in FY26 shifting to modest drag over the next two years
macro_indicators.interpretation: Gridlock is expected to hold federal spending at FY26 levels through continuing resolutions, reducing the fiscal contribution to growth.

risk_factors: Inflation and cost of living remain key political and policy risks and could push the Fed toward a more hawkish response.
Local moratoria or constraints on data center development could delay 2027 AI capex.
Renewed US attacks on Iran in the near term could keep energy prices high.
Budget gridlock and continuing resolutions could make fiscal policy a drag on growth through FY28.

Trump's tariff and military authority is unlikely to change, since Democrats lack a veto-proof 2/3 majority.
